stories.headline: Nuggets beat Bulls 151-145 in overtime on Murray's 45 points in Adelman's 100th game
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets defeated the Chicago Bulls 151-145 in overtime on Sunday at the United Center, earning their first three-game win streak of the season. Jamal Murray scored 45 points, his best start to a season, adding seven assists, five rebounds, three steals and two blocks. Nikola Jokic recorded a triple-double with 37 points, 18 rebounds and 11 assists, the 202nd of his career.

All five Denver starters scored at least 16 points, while the bench combined for just 14. Christian Braun added 21 points, Aaron Gordon 18 and Cam Johnson 16. Denver outscored Chicago 66-48 in the paint but allowed the Bulls to shoot 25 of 55 from three-point range.

Chicago, now 4-12, played without leading scorer Norman Powell and rookie Caleb Wilson. Josh Giddey had 23 points, 22 assists and 14 rebounds, Buddy Hield scored 33 and Jalen Smith added 26 before fouling out.

The game was David Adelman's 100th regular-season game as Nuggets head coach. Denver is 67-33 in that span, a better start than George Karl, Larry Brown or Doug Moe had in their first 100 games with the franchise.

stories.headline: Broncos beat Raiders 38-24 as rookie Jonah Coleman scores three touchdowns
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos earned their ninth victory of the season Sunday, defeating the Las Vegas Raiders 38-24 at Empower Field at Mile High. Rookie running back Jonah Coleman carried 24 times for 111 yards and three touchdowns.

The performance gave the team a lead back it has lacked and raised hopes for a more sustainable offense going forward. The Broncos have now won consecutive games against their division rival.

The game was also an emotional one. Fans gathered ahead of kickoff to remember Tom Jackson, the Ring of Fame linebacker and Orange Crush defense cornerstone, who died unexpectedly Friday evening in Ohio at age 75.

stories.headline: Broncos legend Tom Jackson dies at 75
stories.summary:
Tom Jackson, the Broncos linebacker whose outsized personality and aggressive play made him one of the most beloved players in franchise history, died unexpectedly Friday evening in Ohio. He was 75. A Ring of Fame member, Jackson was a cornerstone of the team's Orange Crush defense.

His daughter Taylor Jackson, a former Broncos public relations intern, notified Broncos Chief Communications Officer Patrick Smyth of her father's death. The family asked that Chris Berman, Jackson's longtime ESPN colleague, deliver the news publicly.

Fans gathered before Sunday's game against the Las Vegas Raiders to honor Jackson, whose impact on the franchise extended well beyond the field. He was a team captain during the 1977 season that sent Denver to its first Super Bowl.

stories.headline: Colorado unemployment rate rises to 4.4% in October, largest jump of 2026
stories.summary:
Colorado's unemployment rate rose to 4.4% in October from 4.1% in September, the biggest monthly increase in more than a year, according to the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment. The national rate fell one-tenth of a point to 4.1%. Denver County's rate was 4.6%.

There are 139,200 unemployed Coloradans, up 7,300 from September, and the number of employed residents fell by 3,000 to 3,044,500. The labor force grew by 4,300, its first increase in the participation rate since 2023, which officials said means more people are entering the workforce but not finding jobs.

Tim Wonhof of CDLE's Office of Labor Market Information called it the largest upward move outside a recession in 40 years and said it seems outsized, so revisions will be closely watched. Seasonal hiring also fell short: the state usually adds about 10,000 jobs in October but lost 5,700, and hospitality shed 3,200 jobs.

stories.headline: More young adults are leaving Denver and Colorado, and fewer are arriving
stories.summary:
Colorado is seeing more young adults depart and fewer arrive, according to a Denver Post analysis of migration data. The shift marks a change from last decade, when a migration wave boosted the state's population by roughly 450,000 people.

The story profiles Adam and Britt Chou, who were part of that earlier wave. Their experience illustrates how the state's pull on young workers has changed.

The trend carries implications for the state's workforce, housing market and economy as Denver-area employers compete for talent.

stories.headline: Colorado commission mandates phaseout of commercial gas lawn equipment to cut ozone
stories.summary:
The Colorado Air Quality Control Commission voted unanimously Friday to phase out gas-powered lawn care equipment used by commercial operators in nine northern Front Range counties during summer months, starting next year. The rule adds to existing restrictions on government parks and landscaping departments.

The vote follows one of the worst ozone seasons in recent years, with sensors recording violations on 66 days, just under the record of 67. State health officials say the lawn and garden sector contributes about 13% of ground-level ozone in the nonattainment area, though mowers, trimmers and blowers account for only a couple of parts per billion against the federal limit of 70.

CoPIRG and other environmental groups praised the decision. Colorado law provides a 30% discount on clean electric equipment at qualified retailers, and the Regional Air Quality Council offers grants to help commercial operators switch.

stories.headline: Fire leaves five City Park West condo units uninhabitable
stories.summary:
A porch fire early Saturday morning left five condominium units uninhabitable in Denver's City Park West neighborhood. No injuries were reported.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Separately, the Colorado State Patrol is increasing patrols to stop dangerous drivers as one of the busiest travel weeks of the year approaches.

stories.headline: Thanksgiving dinner prices rise nationally but drop in Colorado
stories.summary:
The cost of a Thanksgiving dinner is rising nationally this year, but prices have dropped in Colorado, according to a Denver Post report.

The story examines grocery costs, including the price of turkey, for Colorado households planning holiday meals.

The decline offers some relief to Colorado shoppers as the holiday week begins.

stories.headline: Perspective: Colorado's energy future in the balance as new leaders take office
stories.summary:
A Denver Gazette perspective piece urges Gov.-elect Phil Weiser and the incoming General Assembly to weigh the role of oil and natural gas in the state's economy as they consider energy policy.

The piece cites a 2025 analysis finding the industry directly accounted for more than 62,000 Colorado jobs in 2023 and supported nearly 325,000 jobs and $57.5 billion in economic output, nearly 11% of the total. Surveys commissioned by Coloradans for Responsible Energy Development found 82% of likely voters called the industry important to the economy.

It also points to revenue for public services, noting that oil and gas property made up about 95% of assessed value in Weld County's Platte Valley RE-7 School District, and that federal mineral leasing revenue helps fund schools statewide.

topStory.headline: Army Reschedules Lead Azide Detonation at Iowa Munitions Plant for Wednesday Despite Court Stay
topStory.summary:
The U.S. Army said Sunday night it will carry out a controlled detonation of nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday, Nov. 25, citing the need "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced." The date is the second delay of the operation. Two detonations were first scheduled for Nov. 20, then moved to Nov. 23, and a Justice Department filing late Saturday had said the Army intended to act by Nov. 24. The Army did not immediately explain why the timeline shifted, and as of Sunday afternoon it had not posted updated plume models for the new date.

The plan is proceeding despite a pause ordered by the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which granted an administrative stay on an emergency EPA permit after the Iowa Environmental Council, the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter and Earthjustice sued. In a Saturday filing, the Army said it would invoke an emergency munitions and explosives exclusion in EPA regulations that allows the action without a permit. On Sunday, the Justice Department urged the court to lift the stay, arguing that a controlled detonation is "necessary now to respond to the immediate threat of an uncontrolled explosion." The Army said it would follow the permit's mitigation measures even if the permit is not in effect, including steps to limit the spread of lead dust.

The Army says the roughly 9,700 pounds of lead azide, a primary explosive used to initiate munitions, has deteriorated and recrystallized, making it highly sensitive to friction and shock. The EPA said disturbing the containers could create an unacceptable risk of unintentional detonation, and the Army has said moving the material is not safe and that destroying it in place is the only responsible option. The government warned that temperatures expected to fall below 30 degrees could cause further crystallization and increase the risk of a spontaneous explosion, and an Army munitions expert submitted a declaration to that effect. The Army, the EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services said they have been planning since March and will take "the most extreme mitigation measures available." The Army has acknowledged the detonation will produce a dust plume containing some lead, loud noise, ground vibrations and possibly broken windows.

Environmental groups argue the blast could spread lead dust across a wide area, potentially reaching communities more than 100 miles away in Iowa and Illinois. They filed affidavits from scientists and officials on Sunday challenging the Army's justification for proceeding. Sierra Club Iowa Chapter Legal Chair Wally Taylor said the Army "has clearly mishandled this situation" and called for a full review, adding that if detonation is now the only option, affected residents must have access to testing, mitigation and remediation resources. The groups also criticized the lack of public information about the revised plan.

The Army said additional details would be forthcoming, and the 8th Circuit has yet to rule on the Justice Department's request to lift the stay. The outcome will determine whether the detonation proceeds under the EPA permit or solely under the Army's claimed regulatory exclusion, a legal question that may draw further challenge. Attention now turns to weather conditions, the release of updated dispersion models, and the monitoring and testing available to residents in the region after the blasts.
